utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Sarapa and Ms. Condon and Mr. Meek. Yes, Mr. Haynes, is Mr. Sarapa --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa will be here after the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Condon is working from the office. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. And Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. Mr. Meek will be here after the first break as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record also, Prosecution is represented by Mr. McCloskey and present in the courtroom also is the Defence expert sitting next to Mr. Ostojic. The witness is also present. Doctor, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed and hopefully finish within a short time your testimony so you can go back to your beautiful Norway. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, doctor, again.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify a couple issues that we discussed yesterday and then talk about some of the tables in your conclusions section today and I promise I'll speak a little slower and I'll pause before I give you another question and after your answer so I apologise yesterday if I overlapped with you, sir. Sir, when we speak of these informational sources did you or anyone in your staff ever examine the provider of the information which was given to those sources?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't quite understand what you mean, "examine the provider". I could mention each source. The missing lists were provided by two international organisations. We did not examine the people but we talked to many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The census were provided by the statistical office so we certainly had contact with all the owners or the originators of the sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asking that but just so I understand it you used two primary information sources that you discussed that's highlighted in the first paragraph under your executive summary; the ICRC and the PHR, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I classify, and correct me if I'm wrong, the other sources as secondary sources that you utilised in your methodology that we discussed briefly yesterday. But my question is this: With respect to the two primary sources, namely the ICRC and the PHR, did you examine in their data bank from whom they obtained the information which they ultimately gathered upon which you relied? So the provider meaning the person who gave the information to the ICRC or the PHR?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. We examined that and the information was provided by family members in about 95 per cent of the cases for both these primary data sources. We even looked at who of -- what kind of family member, mother, father, grandparents, siblings, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where can I find that analysis?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only gave the summary figure, that 95 per cent were provide by family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you did the analysis. What I'm interested to know is to verify to an extent if it was immediate family members, if it was friends or witnesses that may have identified a person last at a certain place, because that's certainly a category you utilised in your report, or was it distant family members?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, sir, friends and -- are not family members. So they were most of them were close family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I don't want to belabour the point, just one last time, is that data available anywhere that we can examine at all?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is a summary of it but we didn't do any detailed analysis. We found it sufficient to notice that very high proportion, almost all, 19 out of 20, were provided by family members and in most cases, close family members. In some cases there were no family members available to provide the information since they were also killed or missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you have family members, multiple family members, providing the information to those sources?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened in some cases, I think, but this was detected and possible duplicates we deleted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what per cent was that, that multiple family members provided the information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the last 2005 OTP list, I think there were about 24 records, something, where the information was provided more than once, and not deleted by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this: If DNA is the certain form of analysis to determine death and identity of a person, as you described yesterday, you say that there was approximately 7.660 members who supplied blood samples, or people who supplied blood samples to this DNA data bank, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said 7.849.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's why I said about 7 -- okay, 7.849 people provided blood samples to that data bank, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think you also said, and it's pretty well known, that in order to obtain or confirm analysis through blood samples through DNA you have to have more than one family provide a blood sample, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please make a pause between questions and answers, thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probability of a mistake, mistaken identity is much reduced if there are more than one family member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic and Dr. Brunborg, please slow down. I mean -- it's the pause that you ought to allow between question and answer and that applies to both of you. You're creating a lot of problems for the interpreters. So please comply, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you -- may I proceed, Your Honour? Did you, sir, review and analyse the DNA blood sample bank, if you will, or the information that contains those blood samples to determine specifically the number of individuals that provided blood samples for this identification process?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we examined all the information we obtained from ICMP, which included DNA analysis reports on -- on profiles and links and cases et cetera. We were not provided with any information on which family members provided the blood samples, if I am not mistaken, but I'm not 100 per cent sure about that. The ICMP is very protective about the data, which are confidential naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just pausing in order to comply, so when you're done, I'll ask another question.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that gives me time to add on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course it does. Sir, my question is: Do you know or did any organisation provide you a specific amount of the number of individuals that provided blood samples for this DNA identification process? Do you have a fixed number or an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard it but I do not remember now. I went over the report carefully again. I did not see a fixed number but I think there were on average two or three per victim or per missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we have 7.800, sir, people providing blood samples, mathematically although I know you're not a mathematician, wouldn't we divide the 2 into the 7.800 and we can generally estimate that about 3.500 people gave blood samples, or I should say 7.800 people gave blood samples for approximately 3.800 or 3.500 missing people?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, you misunderstood this. 7.800 missing persons as reported by family members, for each of them, between two and three on the average so that comes closer to 20.000 blood samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 or 20.000 blood samples in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding, doctor, however, that the number of blood samples was 7.800 blood samples. Are you telling me now that the blood samples that were procured for this identification process was in excess of 20.000?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the exact number. I never said there were 7.800 blood samples. I said there were 7.800 persons or missing persons for whom blood samples had been obtained by -- from family members. Whether the 15 or 20.000, in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where can I obtain that information, if I wanted to have the exact information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can object -- sorry, break. You can obtain that from ICMP in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you told us that you participated in a census in, I think, four or five different countries. Can you share with us what your role was in your participation in those censuses?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say I participated in those censuses. For some of the censuses, I did some analysis. For others censuses I participated in planning the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you describe for me what you did in the planning of the census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the planning of the census of Albania, for example, I looked at possible links with registers. That was one of my roles there, and how -- we also looked at how it could be used to establish a population register, which was eventually not done. I actually also was part of the consideration of the census of Afghanistan, playing much the same role.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, I want to discuss yesterday you mentioned that you were aware of approximately or up to three ambushes involving the column that was leaving from the Potocari area through towards Tuzla; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked, yes we talked about that. I don't recall saying three ambushes. I knew there were -- I know there were many ambushes. I've read books and seen movies and videos and read reports about ambushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many people died as a result or a consequence of those ambushes?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And it's not given in our report either. It is -- in the report it is listed the number of people who were last seen in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Take a look at page 3 of your report, on the second section identified as "background", the first three lines. And there you talk about these men who tried to escape by walking through the forest and you say that many of them were killed on the way or after surrendering or being captured. As a demographer, sir, first I'd like to know is where you got this information from?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, much of this was documented in other trials also. So it is well known that men -- were killed and I've also seen movies and some have been recovered in graves with pathologists, have been confirmed that they have been shot or killed in other ways. Whether they were killed in an ambush or in some other way, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you write down that they were killed, like you do on the bottom of the page that we clarified yesterday in the objective of your analysis. Would we want to change that to just say died or dead; because you don't know the manner or the cause of death, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says several women, children and old men were also killed. I think it's pretty clear now, history, evidence showed that several were killed. It doesn't say all, it doesn't say many. It says several.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm really referring to the sentence before that though. Not that sentence?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Others were separated from their families in Potocari and later executed." Is that the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The sentence, the first one on that background section and I'll read it, so you can focus with me on. It says: "When the enclave of Srebrenica fell in -- on July -- 11 July 1995, a number of men tried to escape by walking through the forest and many of them were killed on the way or after surrendering or being captured." Okay? That's the sentence I'd like to focus on?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that has been pretty well documented elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, tell me, doctor, how many were killed?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say, and I don't have exact number. This was background. It is not presented as evidence as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So this in the background section should not be looked at by anyone as evidence that you formulated any opinions based upon a reasonable degree of certainty; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's background. It is not -- it does not affect our results because our results does not say anything about who was killed or not how many were killed but we know of course, sir, we know that many were killed since many have been exhumed from mass graves with strong evidence from forensic pathologists that they were, for example, blindfolded and shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I concede that point, sir and we've had the opportunity to discuss with the anthropologists and pathologists no that evidence. But quite a few, if not a greater percentage, of those were not blindfolded and did not have bindings or ligatures on their hands. I won't debate the issue with you. I just want to know, sir, how do you know that they were killed or on the way or after surrendering, who provided you with that information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information I've read in other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, we discussed a classification of combat or war activities and one of the classifications that you have or two groups is battle-related and non-battle-related. Can you tell me the significance of the first classification, battle-related deaths, what's the significance of that, since it appears in your article and you're considered by some colleagues at least to be a forensic demographer?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Battle deaths is a military concept and it's also used in some -- it is used to give a total account, to -- excuse me, to say to define a war or a civil conflicts. This is why it was collected. Definition of a civil conflict is at least 25 battle deaths per year. A definition of a war is at least 1.000 battle deaths per year. So that is one of the uses of that concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But isn't another use of the concept and the real use of the concept to distinguish between battle-related deaths and non-battle-related deaths is because battle-related deaths have perhaps a legitimate and justified result?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it's legitimate or justified, I will not say anything about but, of course, as both of us know, it is not considered a war crime usually to be killed in a battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So battle-related deaths are not considered a war crime for both soldiers and civilians, because you include both in your categorisation, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I think I'm now you are leading me into thin legal ice which I will prefer not to go deeply into.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just trying to understand your articles and your thoughts on it because you've written several. Now, do you agree with me, sir, that though, that you can have within a civil war both battle-related deaths and non-battle-related deaths, deaths that occur whether a battle didn't happen on a given day or week, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But of course being a soldier and being killed is not the same as being -- dying in a battle. A soldier could die in a car accident or from disease. So somebody who is not a soldier could also die, could die in an ambush. So it is -- there is not a one-to-one relationship between being a soldier and dying in a conflict, and a battle-related death.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To what extent in your analysis, since you make some of these conclusions and what I consider to be broad statements, did you utilise the office of the Prosecution and any other department such as the military analysts that were creating this data to see if it was a legitimate military battle death or a non-battle death?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as you know, we were not tasked to identify battle deaths or not in this context, only the number of dead and missing persons so this is purely written as background material for the setting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think this has been gone through thoroughly yesterday and today. Any further on this is really getting cumulative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic? What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This specific general area was but we've covered many areas generally speaking. We have never discussed in his report specifically on this page 3 under background, that first sentence that we were discussing now. If that's specific to a general statement that we made yesterday, I'll concede we did discuss the classifications that he himself acknowledges, that Mr. Butler also includes and I think it's time to go specific now, to analyse his report in that context. So I disagree respectfully with my learned friend that that has been gone over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think given the time that Mr. Ostojic has had on these subjects that, I think, his time should be just about run out. I don't know what he means, "going specific". The first paragraph -- the first paragraph, "When the enclave of Srebrenica fell on 11 July a number of men tried to escape by walking through the forest and many of them were killed", is he contesting that? Why are we going over this and over this and over this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our agreement is that we continue beating around the same bush and we've been doing that for a long, long time. Especially since you are not the first Defence counsel to cross-examine this witness. And some of the questions you are putting have already been put by others, and answered too. So if you could bring this to a conclusion, please, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I ask one more question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, doctor, that you did not review or discuss with any military analyst from the Office of the Prosecutor such as Richard Butler to determine what -- whether any of the deaths that you identify and of those that are missing were battle-related or non-battle-related?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I knew Mr. Butler but it was not relevant for our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, because of the Court's obvious ruling, I'll move on to another subject. If I can direct your attention to page 15 of your report, table 1 specifically, I'd like to examine the ICRC categories that you have listed down there. Do you see them?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Category number 2 you have: "Still missing, with info on death". Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that there is a body that is linked to the body of the missing person, has been found or identified somehow but it has not gone through all the legal procedures, saying taken to the case -- the case has not been taken to a court so that the death certificate has been issued. This is when the relative is notified. That is when the ICRC closes a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I see those categories there. But is this the ICRC categorisation or is this your own? Because on the one immediately above that you have "Still missing", and it doesn't say whether they have information on death or no information on death. Then we have the closed cases which are confirmed deaths of 2.054. So really my question focuses on the "Still missing". Compare that to the "Still missing, with information on death".

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the "Still missing", there is no information beyond the one provided by relatives about the whereabouts or the fate of these persons. "Still missing, with info on death", there is information about body. But it has not gone through the legal process. That is my understanding and this is the definition given by ICRC, and they print different tables for these cases, different cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Categories?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Categories, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Turning your attention to page 23 of your report, table 7, just a couple questions. I know were you asked this yesterday but I need to clarify this point with the Court's indulgence and permission and the Prosecutor's, of course. Under the unknown category you have 999; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Speakers overlapping] male and 31 female.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What does that specifically mean? Let me tell you what I think it means, and you tell me if I'm wrong or right and that might be easier, okay?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That means that someone gave as a provider, information to one of the two sources, an individual's name, and when you went and did this match or linking methodology to confirm it with the census you were unable to find that individual with any reasonable degree of certainty, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the PHR database, which includes more than 5.000 people their ethnicity was reported so it's for the remaining between 2 and 3.000 that information was captured from the census through linkage on an individual basis. And as we discussed yesterday, for 13 per cent of the cases, we were not able to link the missing list to the census for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understood it a little. Turning your attention to table 11, my confusion on table 11 is twofold, I think. It's on page 29. My first question is: The category that you have on the left side, the age in 1995, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you don't include any age for children under the age of 10, which may, if you don't really study demography can mean one of two things, one, that no one under the age of 10 was alive at that time or, two, in my view, that the exclusion of all people who were under the age of 10 was done so that you can inflate the percentages on the right-hand side of the column, which is what statisticians and demographers may do from time to time?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. The reason is that there were no missing persons under age 10, no reported. That is why we did not need that category. I could have included it and put zero. The inflation of zero would still be zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you're comparing this with the 1991 census population, are you not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when you do that type of comparative analysis shouldn't you include the entire group of all ages, if you're going to compare 1995 to 1991?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we would have seen that zero per cent of the 1991 population of persons under the age of 10 were reported as missing. Whether inflated or not. We remember, excuse me, that we inflate the number of missing persons by 13 per cent, not the 1991 population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think it would be a more reasonable approach to have the absolute numbers for these age groups as they existed in 1991 for this chart to be more complete, because we can get that information obviously by looking at the census; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's available. I think it has also been printed in one of our earlier reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't find it at all.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you find it in my article on this? "Accounting for genocide"? I thought it was included there but -- no, we did not include the absolute numbers there either, for limitations of space.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about the totality of the number? Would that influence or impact the percentages that you've offered here to show as a percentage of the whole, if you don't include the whole, you can get an inflated percentage, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the way here when it is zero in those age groups, it would not influence the total.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I respectfully disagree but we'll hopefully talk about that at another time. Let me ask you about methodology?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that you're also not a mathematician.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm actually a lawyer. Let me talk about methodology a little bit. You discuss and you call your methodology a match methodology, both in your paper and in your report. I've seen from other people such as Dr. Tabeau, that in fact she calls it a link methodology and we discussed briefly that. I submit to you, sir, that your methodology is not a match methodology but a link methodology and that the reason you don't want to call it a linkage or link methodology is because it has less reliability?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that terminology doesn't really matter whether you call it linking or matching. We have used interchangeably. If you really go into the terminology, maybe you find some -- you could find some difference in the interpretation but it's really the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I don't -- again, fair enough. The data that you used to make the comparisons between the various sources were not matched because you didn't have all the data or the same data from each of the sources, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data were deficient. That is why we did not succeed in linking or matching the whole population. Where we think there -- it should have been close to 100 per cent linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's a lot of information to digest but I think I understand but my point is exactly that. I don't want to use the words interchangeably. To match something, you would have five key features, for example, that you utilised from a source. And then during your methodology, you would see if you could match or link this person and you can match them only if you have the five features that correspond to one another; correct? That would be considered a match. A link would be if you have five features from one source, and you try to compare it with this other source and you can only link two out of those five. That would be a link, would it not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree entirely. I think what we are linking actually is -- or is different records, to see if two different records are for the same, are most likely for the same person and we are using different measures, different variables, to see if it is likely or unlikely that these two different records represent the same person or not. If, sir, if you have a perfect system, like a good identification number system like in the Nordic countries, there is no doubt. We use one variable, the Nordic maticni broj to do the linking. We do not need to worry about spelling mistakes in names, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just look here, I had a couple other questions. Yes. Still on page 29, it's table 11, but I want to move away from table 11 and go to the bottom of figure 5. And although this may have been covered and if the Court permits, I'll ask the question and I'm sure it may draw an objection, although we didn't discuss it yesterday or today. You talk about in that figure 5 on page 29, deaths from war related causes, do you not? It's the very last line on that page.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You talk about deaths from natural causes; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then if you flip the page you have other phenomenons. That I suggest, sir, is another hint that, in fact, you as a forensic demographer were placing in this report but yet didn't complete the analysis that we so desperately need here in this courtroom. But what's the significance, if you will, of identifying just as a broad category deaths from war related causes in your demographic report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: These four bullet points are a discussion of the possible loss of the population, 1991 population - there was a census in all of Bosnia in 1991 - here specifically in Srebrenica. And what could have happened to those people who were enumerated there. Here we talk about Muslim men. Now, they could go -- be -- go missing from in the conflict related to the fall of Srebrenica, and die in that conflict, reported as missing. They could die from natural causes. They could have left Srebrenica before 12th of July 1995. Or they could go fighting elsewhere. These were the major reasons. Now, what we have looked at here is just those who went missing and who are most likely dead. More and more evidence points in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where would you --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we see, if I may continue, we see then that of those men who were 45 to 49, fully 50 per cent of those who were -- who lived in Srebrenica in 1991 were reported as missing and are most probably dead. Half of the Muslim men in Srebrenica in 1991 died most probably. That is a very large percentage. When we do not consider those who were not exposed to the risk of killing or execution or disappearing in July 1995, because they were not there before Srebrenica fell, so the real percentage is probably much higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you show me where, in your work, that you actually broke down these four bullet points to give us an indication as to what the percentages were for each of those four bullet points?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will very much like to do so, sir, but we have no information about those other bullet points. I would like to make a full account of the fates of all those who were enumerated in 1991 but we only have indications about those who went missing in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just couple more questions. On your table 11 we talked about the need to have absolute numbers from 1991 in that table. You'll agree with me - won't you? - that if we know that in 1991 there was approximately let's say, I don't know, you have 0.4 amount of people in Srebrenica for that category, which I don't understand fully, either you have one or you have -- you can't have less than one, but I'm sure a statistician or a mathematician could help me with that better. But my question is: If you take the category in 1991 and in any given group you've identified here by age, 15 to 19, let's say, in 1991 that age group 15 to 19, there were 100 people --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- what happens to that age group in 1995?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, it is four years older. Secondly, 31.7 per cent of them were reported as missing and have probably died so about one third went missing. The other two-thirds we do not know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But what days are you using for that four-year period or to categorise people being exactly 20 or 15 to 19? Because obviously some can be 19 this year, and some can turn 19 the following year.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Age in 1995", so if they were 15 to 19 in 1995 then they were 11 through 15 in 1991 so that is the number we looked at, the original age group was 11 through 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you yesterday about the quality of the primary and secondary sources that were used, and how significant that may be to assess their credibility or reliability. And I have the same question with the methodology you used, whether it's matching or linkage methodology that you utilised. Isn't it important that the quality of that methodology is important to assess the extent of credibility and reliability and value if any we can have on the conclusions that you set forth in your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, the methodology is very important, and I think we did a pretty good job on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, doctor. I look forward to seeing you again. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. According to the latest verification, I have the Popovic and Miletic team who wish to cross-examine the witness. I see Ms. Fauveau standing. Go ahead, Madam Fauveau. You've asked for 20 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke about the census in 1991 in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is it true that in 1991, the information was collected for the census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. The census day, as we call it, the reference day, was 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the information that was collected in 1991 was published in 1995, because it took that long to process that information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly correct. Some preliminary results were published earlier but because of the conflicts, the first big volume was published in Zagreb, in fact, on the basis of data from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And Zagreb is in Croatia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you ever envisage a possibility that the result of the census that was published in Zagreb in Croatia could have been tampered with in any way?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we considered that. Now, we did in fact have access to the full data set with data on the 4.3 million individuals that were enumerated and we made tabulations and compared with the Zagreb publication and found very few differences. There were a few but very minimal. It was mostly very much the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that after the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was no census of the population, the Muslim and the Croatian population, in the part called the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. There are plans for holding a census, and the statistical agency would very much like to do so. I met with them. It is highly needed for planning purposes and other purposes, but the Office of the High Representative does not allow it before certain political conditions have been met, such as the return of refugees and displaced persons. They are afraid that a census might in a way cement a population situation that is not considered desirable.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But at the same time, in Republika Srpska, there was some sort of a census carried out?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with that, but I have not seen -- I have not had access to the individual data from that census. Was there something in 1995? Was there something? I do not recall the exact date but there was some kind of a census. Whether it was conducted according to national standards, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe that it was in 1997 [as interpreted], and what is interesting, it is the fact that the census was carried out in Republika Srpska and it wasn't carried out in the federation. And it was in 1996, I believe it was recorded wrongly in the transcript. So does that strike you as strange?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. Any government would like to have a census of the population. So if they managed to do that, that is -- that's excellent. But if I may add, that this was not a national census, it was a census of a part of the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you never thought that a census was not carried out in the federation because the authorities in the federation wanted to hide certain information that might have been revealed by a census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That did not strike my mind. In fact, I met with the director of the statistical office. I met with the three-headed directors of the statistical agency at the same time. One -- two from the federation, one Croat and one Muslim and one Serb from the Republika Srpska, and we discussed the possibility of the census. They all wanted that. And I met also with the federal director separately. They all wanted very much a census. Whether there could have been political pressure to avoid a census, I have no idea but that was never my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I am sorry to keep you waiting. I'm waiting for the interpretation to be over before I ask my next question. But in your work, you never had an opportunity to discuss the census at the political level, at a high political level, for example, with any of the ministers or the Prime Minister or any such figures?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: To hold a census was not really part of my mandate, but I -- but I did not have that opportunity, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On 1st February of this year, when you testified in this Court, you stated that you were involved in a new discipline that could be called the demography of armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And yesterday you have told us that your first task when you started to work for the Office of the Prosecutor was to evaluate the demographic facts of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The translation should be the demographic implications or effects of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the demographic effects of a war or an armed conflict also include immigrations, emigrations and the movement of people?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. It could also include births, and marriages, and divorces, and splitting of families.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we say that an armed conflict provokes any movement of people, that emigration from a country is more pronounced during an armed conflict or a war, as opposed to the state of peace? Just to be more precise, I said migrations or any movement of people.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a normal case. If there are other countries that are willing to receive people from the country that is in a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you evaluate such movements, are you able to distinguish between forced migrations and spontaneous migrations of the population in a country struck by war?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very -- can be very hard. Now, of course, for people who are received or taken care of by refugee organisations like the United Nations High Commission of Refugees, then that is usually forced migration but whether a person is migrating, say, even in Bosnia, to work in another country or to seek refuge because he or she was feeling threatened or had lost their house or job, it's difficult to tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, can we say that during a conflict or during a war, one part of the population seeks to leave the area struck by the conflict spontaneously, without being forced to do so?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If they can do so. Now, I can think of cases where they were not -- it was not possible, in, say, Srebrenica in 1995 it was not possible for the population in the town of Srebrenica to leave is my understanding. Another area of conflict where it is difficult for population to leave is of course Palestine, the West Bank and Gaza, and we can think of all the cases where many would like to leave and are not allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I clarify the transcript? Did you say, doctor, it was not possible for the population in the town of Srebrenica to leave or to live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To leave, to depart from Srebrenica. There was a-- it was considered a safe enclave and the people were, they were supposed to be protected, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that it was not possible to leave the area of Srebrenica, are you aware of the fact that people did leave Srebrenica before the 14th of July 1995? Before July 1995, without a date.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some left, I think, and there were periods when there were people were allowed to leave, there were periods where people were encouraged to leave and other periods where they were told not to leave. There were periods where they were -- they could not leave because there were guards against it. So I do not remember all the period from 1992 to 1995 but it was changing. There was also periods when people went into Srebrenica from surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you say that it was not possible to leave Srebrenica in 1995, what you actually mean is that it was difficult to leave Srebrenica, not impossible?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have spoken about a part of the population that had arrived in Srebrenica. Would you agree that people who had arrived in Srebrenica arrived in 1991 and 1992 at the very beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the history of all the flows and the local events in that area. But if I may add, the data on the missing persons show that many of the people who went -- reported as missing came from other municipalities surrounding so they must have arrived in Srebrenica before 11 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that you do not have facts or information that would allow us to assess the ratio between the population that immigrated into Srebrenica as opposed to those who emigrated from Srebrenica in the period between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I wish I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But, as you said it on the 1st of February, you believed that a lot of Muslims left Srebrenica before 1995. This is what you stated in front of this Trial Chamber on the 1st of February; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On several occasions, you have stated and written in various reports that the number of persons living in Srebrenica at the time was 40.000. That was an evaluation on your part and on the part of other people.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, as you said, an evaluation of United Nations, reported, mentioned yesterday. It was not my evaluation. That was -- the 40.000 was the only figure I had. No breakdown, either breakdown by sex, age, ethnicity, country of normal residence, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In fact, would it be your opinion that that number for the greatest part is based on rumours, on stories more than anything?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the origin of the number, whether it was based on lists for -- to get provisions for the isolated population in the enclave or rumours or not. So I don't know how good that estimate is. As I said yesterday, I've tried and talked to many people about the existence of such lists but never been able to obtain any.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember from the Blagojevic case, when you testified on the 3rd of February 2004, that you stated that the 40.000 persons is based on rumours? Let me read back the phrase to you -- the question was whether there were 40.000 people in Srebrenica and your answer was as follows: [In English] "That's what the rumours say."

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is approximately the same thing as I said now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it also true that part of that number of 40.000 is estimated based on the estimates of various humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This has been spent a lot of time on before. This is really repetitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau, would you move to something else, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very important for my client, and I would like to ask Your Honours' leave to continue this line of questioning, and I would also like to ask the Chamber to extend my time because of the interpretation that is taking a bit longer, and I would not like to be at a disadvantage as opposed to my colleagues who speak the same language as the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will certainly not be allowed to put any repetitive questions from now on, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not intend to repeat my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what you have asked the witness he has already answered and possibly spent more than 45 minutes since he first started giving evidence on cross-examination, and that was 189 minutes, 3 hours and nine minutes, he spent on cross-examination so far, of which I reckon one hour was spent precisely on the matters that you are asking him now. He's given ample evidence -- I'm not here to argue, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am -- I do not intend to enter any arguments. I would like to show the witness a document that has already been shown to him and I assure you I don't intend to repeat my questions. I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit number 2D3. Could we show the witness paragraph number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in front of me from yesterday. I was given to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify certain things. You said this was an estimate. I'm not going to ask you that again. According to this document, we cannot even determine whether this is an estimate from 1993, the beginning of that year, or the end of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This is extremely repetitive on an issue that has -- the probative value of which was explained by this witness. I think we can expect some kind of coordination on an issue like this from the Defence so that we avoid this sort of repetitiveness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, if the penultimate sentence of the same paragraph that you refer the witness to says precisely, "In 1993 UNPROFOR estimated the population of Srebrenica to be 42.000. By a process of deduction, it can therefore be determined that approximately 17.000 DPs are currently accounted for," how can you put to the witness that according to this document, we cannot even determine whether this is an estimate from 1993, the beginning of that year or the end of that year?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. Mr. President, what I would like to know is this estimate of 40.000 people, this is not the people who have gone missing. This is an estimate of the people that lived in Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered. I mean Mr. Ostojic himself asked him questions on how he made his estimates, on the basis of which, and Mr. Zivanovic -- not Mr. Zivanovic, Madam Nikolic yesterday asked him the same question so where are we heading? I'm not going to let you have the witness go through all these figures again one by one, once he has already testified upon it. I mean, if the witness happened to be one who wavers, who is doubtful or is, or who doesn't know what he is testifying about, I could tolerate that but he's been asked these questions repetitively already. We have been very patient. Mr. McCloskey has been less patient than we have been. We have been patient precisely because we don't like to interrupt you as much as we can, but obviously there comes a point when we have to set a limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think that this particular question has been asked, but in any case, I'll move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that you spoke to UNHCR after having obtained the list of persons who lived in Srebrenica before the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe something got lost in the translation. I had not obtained a list of people who lived in Srebrenica in 1995, nor in 1993, as the previous document referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe that we have a problem with the interpretation, you're right. Yesterday you said, on page 85 of the transcript, that you believed that you could address the UNHCR in order to be able to obtain the list of people who had resided in Srebrenica before the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point, I believe so, but the approaches from the Office of the Prosecutor to UNHCR did not succeed in anything, in any concrete list. Estimating the number of people in a population, say, based on head counts, counts of houses, five or ten people in each house, is completely different from having a list with a name and date of birth of everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember, when you testified in the Blagojevic case, on the 3rd of February and you said that the UNHCR did not wish to provide any information concerning individual people?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They want to consider the privacy of individuals and also be considered a neutral organisation. So for a long time I could not -- I was not allowed to contact UNHCR directly. It has to -- it had to go through the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that you spoke to the mothers of Srebrenica. You said that yesterday. Did you talk to them yourself or through somebody else?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sorry, a translation again. Yesterday I said I talked to the mayor of Srebrenica but I did in fact also meet with the mothers of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The mayor of Srebrenica. The mayor of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I met the newly elected mayor of Srebrenica in Tuzla in 1999, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you give us his name, please?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you spoke to that person, did you talk to him as a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you record his statement? Did you make a note of what was said during that meeting, a written note?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, that it was included in my report from that trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you did not make an official statement or an official note of that meeting, minutes of sorts?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, particularly because it did not result in anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 1st of February, this year, you said that the number of those people who went missing in Potocari is over 2.000. Is it true that the place where they went missing is based on the information that was gathered by the Red Cross organisation?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, from family members of those who went missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it also true that the Red Cross could not ask very exact questions of the people who reported that members of their families went missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand your question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm referring to your report dated 12th February 2000, which is Exhibit number P571, page 3.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a paragraph immediately above the title, "The quality of the International Committee of the Red Cross" and you say in this paragraph, "[In English] ICRC did not pose any precise question to the families but defined Srebrenica-related victims on the basis of the story given by the informant."

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Unlike the PHR, in the paragraph immediately above, which asked specifically if the person in -- disappeared after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995. But also at the end of this paragraph you just read, it says, "The story given by the informant usually starts with, during the fall of Srebrenica or after the fall of Srebrenica." However this information was not provided to us by the ICRC. We would have liked to have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When it comes to the place of disappearance, this is based on the information that was provided to you by the Red Cross, and this in turn was based on the information provided to them by those who reported their persons went missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to you and what you know, this was never checked, the place of disappearance was never checked by anybody?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We checked it as much as we could. In several ways. We checked where it was on the map, whether it was in the vicinity of Srebrenica. And we compared it with the similar information in the PHR database. Whether it was -- if it was far away from Srebrenica, a person who with that place of missing would not be reported. Later, from the exhumations data we know whether the person, whether this was the case or not, whether they disappeared, this information was correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the place of disappearance could have been determined as the place where the person who had been declared missing was seen for the last time? Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: For example, if a person was seen for the last time in Potocari on the 11th of July 1995, you did not have any information to confirm whether that person had gone to the UN base in Potocari or whether that person had continued walking through the forest in the direction of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but my understanding is that people who started-- who walked, started walking, did that from the town of Srebrenica, not from Potocari, where there were many soldiers who looked -- who guarded the people who had collected there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When it comes to the date of people's disappearance, is it possible that there is a percentage of error, for example, people disappeared on the 14th and they were reported as gone missing on the 15th or the 12th?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, but the definition is last seen alive, or it says in footnote 6 on the document you referred to, last seen -- the place last seen alive or there was an eyewitness. In some cases that was also the case. I remember that this was in a conflict situation so it was not like people just walking off to go home or anywhere. In footnote 5, it says - sorry - "This could either be the date the informant him or herself last saw the person alive, or a date based on the information provided by an eyewitness through the informant."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the Red Cross list does not contain the names of the persons who were declared missing? Or who reported that -- who reported on the persons who went missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They have the information, I believe, but they are very protective about that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Fauveau, because this needs to be cleared. Your question, as I understand it, you then corrected it as you went along but it still is, as it shows up in the transcript, and I want to make sure that the witness has answered your question as it was corrected. Your question as it appears on the transcript is, is it true that the Red Cross list does not contain the names of the persons who were declared missing? This is the first question. And then we have or who reported that -- who reported on the persons who went missing. The witness's answer is: "That's correct, they have the information, I believe, but they were -- are very protective about that kind of information." So what did the Red Cross list contain? Did it contain the names of the persons who went missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but not of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not of the informants.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not of the informants. Does that make it clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When it comes to the Red Cross list, do you know when the first report was made on a missing person, when a missing person was reported for the first time?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you were speaking at the same time so we don't have in the transcript Mr. McCloskey's intervention and Madam Fauveau, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to correct a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I would like to know: When was the first piece of information collected about the missing persons? Was that very soon after the events that took place in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my understanding, when people started to arrive in Tuzla, the ICRC started questioning people or people would come forward and report family members as missing. This started very soon after 11th of July. But as you know also, the ICRC had already started in 1992, in the former Yugoslavia, to make reports on missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And after that, the Red Cross updated that list on several occasions and published those lists on several occasions after that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I would like to know, for example, if a person was declared missing in July 1995, immediately after the events in Srebrenica, which had to do something with Srebrenica, and who reappeared in December 1995, for example, would the person, the informant who reported that person missing in the first place be obliged to come back to the Red Cross and correct the original information and declare that person not missing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you informed enough to be able to give an answer to this question, Dr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say that I don't think people were obliged but that they felt a moral responsibility and also that ICRC collected information about survivors in many -- from many different sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think we can have a break now, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one more question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you cannot exclude a possibility that certain people who were on the original list reappeared and this was never registered so it is possible that some of the names are still on the list although those people did not really go missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, of course, possible. The first list we used was published in January 1997. So one and a half years after the events. And I think that most people who were in fact not dead and had reappeared would be taken off the lists. And we have been very careful to compare different lists and compare sources of survivors to eliminate people who were survivors.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President, I would like to thank you for your patience. I would like to consult with my client, who has signalled to me that he wanted to consult with me, and as a result of that, I might have an additional question after the break but for the time being, this is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. If that's the case, you will have every opportunity, Ms. Fauveau. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's move to Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor. First of all, let me ask you about the Red Cross lists and I only will have one question because my colleagues have exhausted quite a lot of topics with regard to those lists. You said that in 95 per cent of the cases, the disappearances were reported by family members. Do you have any information as to whether these family members had been with the missing person in Srebrenica at the time or were those some other family members that had been out of Srebrenica at the moment when that person went missing? Would you know that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We have no information about that. As was described in footnotes referred to, place and date of last seen could have been either through a witness or observed by the family member itself. So I think there are both cases. In most cases my understanding was that the family members were with the person but in other cases they may not have been with the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, you don't have precise information about that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross may have precise information on that but we do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you did not get an insight into the information that the Red Cross has. You didn't inspect that information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We requested all the information they had but we only -- they only sent us what was publicly available anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to a different topic now. The Srebrenica enclave was in existence for about two years and three months. Could you please tell us, or make an estimate or perhaps be more specific about it, whether the number of population in Srebrenica, from its inception until its fall, rise, stay at the same level or decrease?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an increase from 1991. If this estimate of 40.000 in 1995 is correct, then I am -- it was something more than 30.000, I think, enumerated in 1991 but that was for the whole of the municipality of Srebrenica. I do not recall the estimate of -- from the census of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was not quite clear. Let me repeat: What I'm interested in is the period for the Srebrenica enclave, the town and the villages around it, from April 1993, so not 1991, from 1993 until the fall of the enclave in 1995.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but we do not have any information about the exact flows of the population size in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you couldn't even give us an estimate on whether the population figures rose, decreased or stayed at approximately the same level?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression is that it was increasing during that period because of the inflow of people from surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any substantial inflow -- influx of the population into the Srebrenica enclave from the time when it first came into being until its fall?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no exact figures but the list of missing persons include many people who resided in other municipalities in 1991 and most likely moved to Srebrenica then after 1991. Probably during 1993, 1994 and 1995 period. But we have no exact information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have some other information that the enclave was encircled from its inception and it was not easy to get into the enclave. That's why I asked you if you could explain to us what is the basis for your estimates that the population figures rose from the time when the enclave was set up until its fall. But you gave us your answer at any rate. I also saw -- in fact, yesterday you answered and today you repeated that from the international organisations and the BH authorities, you had sought lists of people who had lived in the Srebrenica enclave while it was in existence, and possibly from international organisations, probably regarding the refugees that had been registered after the fall of the enclave, but you said that you did not receive such information. If I understood you correctly, you personally did not seek this information but this was done through the Office of the Prosecutor. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct but I also asked myself organisations and persons who were knowledgeable about this. I really doubt the existence of such lists. I don't think there ever existed complete lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me who did you personally contact regarding those lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, as I said, the mayor of Srebrenica, various organisations in Srebrenica, I think I talked to the statistical office in Sarajevo, the Office of the High Representative, the OSCE, the Red Cross, a number of different -- some ministries, several ministries, the MUP also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And please tell me, in those talks, since you were told that no such lists had been made and you realised that there were no reliable lists, I assume that you were given some data as to the figures for the number -- the number of people who were actually there but you did not take these figures to be reliable because there were no such lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This figure about 40.000 was mentioned several times, but, as I said, I did not receive any lists, which is what we needed really. We needed lists of people or names, not the total figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at Defence Exhibit 1D312. This is a very short document. It has not been translated yet. It's been submitted for translation but since it is very brief I will read it to you and you will get the translation from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it in e-court or not yet?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, it's not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not in e-court, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's been submitted one or two days -- in fact yesterday. So could we then please put this document on e-court? I'm sorry, no. What I meant was -- could you please zoom in so that we can see the document? Could you maybe zoom out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What perhaps is more important is that it is properly focused because I can barely decipher the letters. I don't know if it's the document itself which is blurred but...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it's actually quite clear. The copy is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Congratulations on your eyesight. It means that mine is going bonkers. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a document drafted on the 11th of January 1994. It was addressed to the office of statistics of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the section for statistics in Tuzla, and the district Defence Secretariat in Tuzla and it reads as follows: "On the basis of your document number 031-01/3 dated the 7th of January 1994, we hereby submit the data you requested. The number of the local population in the municipality, 9.791. The number of local population dislocated from their homesteads within the municipality, 10.756. And the number of displaced population from other municipality, 16.708. "Note, we submit the data you have requested for statistical purposes and you should not be providing this information to international organisations because we have the calculation based on the figure of 45.000 people. "The President of the Presidency of the Srebrenica municipality." Professor, I believe that you've not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you've ever been given these figures by the office of statistics from Sarajevo, from Tuzla or from any of the ministries that you've -- that you'd contacted but I assume that even if you had been given these data you would not have thought them reliable because they would not have been accompanied by lists of the persons who are counted here; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And moreover, I don't see how relevant these are. This is for -- dated 7th of January 1994, fully one and a half years before the events took place. So a lot could have happened between January 1994 and July 1995. So in that context, I do not see what -- it is not irrelevant but it's not of course a reliable estimate of the population in Srebrenica in 1995, July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in any case talking of 37.255.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's leave that aside. What I am interested in, this is a figure that is not substantiated by a list and I understand your mistrust as a scientist, as a scholar, but in my view, when you do research, you can select the documents that you want to base your research and the subsequent paper on. In this case, you were tasked with providing a report for this Court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this means that your findings will be checked by the Court and the information that you based your finding on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, that the Court may reach different conclusions and may give probative value to some documents that you yourself did not consider to be valuable; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this case, no, because I never -- I've not seen this document before.
