It also in your translation it said that this document was -- these figures were not to be provided to any international organisation and since I then worked for an international organisation I was not provided with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I showed you this document is because as for the reliability of all the documents, all the information that you got from no matter what source, you based your assessment of the reliability of -- on the presence or absence of such lists, and I showed this to you because I wanted to put it to you that perhaps there wasn't an interest on the part of some party not to provide such lists to you and let me remind you of something else. Yesterday, you told us that the federation MUP had a list, but that you did not take it to be reliable because of the chaotic situation in which this list had been made. Do you remember saying that? I think it's at page 85, line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. These are getting long and confusing. The witness is making a best effort to answer what he thinks is being asked and this is creating confusion in the record. I've not been objecting to it but if we can get short, concise answers, I think we could get through this -- questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you come to your question, Mr. Zivanovic, and then we'll see whether it's clear enough or whether we need you to explain it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you stated here that you had been given a list from the BH federation MUP. It's a list for the population in Srebrenica. But that it was your assessment that the list was unreliable because it had been made in a chaotic situation, to paraphrase what you yourself stated at page 85, line 11, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I do not think that I said that I got a list for Srebrenica. MUP provided me with some lists of the population of Bosnia, but no particular list for Srebrenica, as far as I can remember, and no particular list for Srebrenica 1995, July. Moreover, what I looked at, the MUP register or list were not that good, I think. That was my impression in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And was this list submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor, the list that you assessed to be unreliable? Did you have any opportunity to actually look at it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got a file, electronic file, with -- through the Office of the Prosecutor on some part of the population of Bosnia. I do not remember what date they referred to. No, this is too long ago and we found out -- quickly decided that this was either of a little relevance or of poor quality. One reason could be that many variables were missing and it was very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also received from international organisations and national bodies, some assessments or claims as to the number of population that were not substantiated by lists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to point to, in order to remove any doubts about your findings, perhaps it would have been good if you had appended the documents that you yourself did not consider to be reliable or relevant, and enabling us and the Court to assess their value. Don't you think that it would have been a good idea?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we cannot append or include everything received. Then we would have to include thousands and thousands of pages. You have to focus on what we think is interesting and relevant and of good quality, and for the estimation of the number of dead or missing after the fall of Srebrenica, these are the lists that were not relevant or not useful or not sufficiently good quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me now whether the decision not to include the list that you deemed to be irrelevant in your report or not to base your findings on the data that you considered to be unreliable, was made by you or was this done in accordance with certain conditions or terms for your expert report that was made to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done -- these decisions were made by me consulting can colleagues on the basis of my professional experience as to the relevance, et cetera. For example, you mentioned lists. We had a list of the complete census of Bosnia, with 4.3 million records. Are you indicating that we should have included those 4.3 million records, appended that to our report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. You don't have to repeat that. You've already stated that. Thank you. That's not what I meant. I was talking about some documents, and some data, that you assessed to be unreliable but you may have given us the opportunity to look at them and to assess them and I assume that you would then decide not to include something on the same basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This -- counsel has had every opportunity to request whatever he wanted from us for years now and has not. So the implication in that question is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Zivanovic? Or do you wish to pass on to your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I got from the Prosecution everything that they disclosed to us. I didn't know what I should ask. I thought that they had disclosed to us everything that was related to this report. I don't think that every time we get a piece of evidence from the Prosecution, we don't have to then ask them to give us all the other things that they held back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think basically we need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let me move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, once you have stated what you have stated, I think we need to make one thing clear, that we are talking here of good practice for the purpose of the survey or study that was conducted by the witness, and you're suggesting that good practice would be that such a report would contain n the form of appendix, not only the documents that he and his team would have relied upon but also all other documents that they would have completely discarded as being unreliable. I don't know if there is any such good practice that would cover also what you have suggested. I mean, perhaps, the witness can enlighten us on that. I am not an expert on the kind of studies, surveys, that they conduct, so perhaps you can clarify this. Do you know of any practice in your field where those sources that are considered to be unreliable, discarded, are also appended to the report, together with the sources that you choose to rely upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you give a very good summary of that. It is not good practice and not considered scientific practice to include something that is irrelevant. It's considered irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to clarify, I think there is -- should be a distinction drawn between appending numerous data and merely for purposes of thoroughness and completeness. I think the question with your permission should be: Should he include in the report or is there a practice to include in the report other sources that they've, because of their decision, decided not to rely upon and not to include it, but to say we've identified several other sources, we feel they are not reliable, but here are the sources that we have identified. And then we would have asked or he can identify in his report why they were not so reliable. I think that would be the more clearer question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly different from the way Mr. Zivanovic put it. Do you wish to comment on that, Dr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, but it is not scientific practice to include or even mention reports that were of no relevance or not used at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, perhaps you may proceed to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now look at another document. That's 1D314. I hope it is in e-court. But let me give you the English version because it's been translated, just page 1. Could you please look at paragraph 3 -- no, I'm sorry, first of all, you will see that this is a document of the 8th Operations Group of Srebrenica, the date is the 9th of September 1994. It is addressed to the 2nd Corps, the security department in Tuzla. It's a weekly report. Could you please look at paragraph 3? 3(a), just (a). Second sentence, which reads, "A mass exodus from the enclave is underway. About 1.200 people have left the enclave in the last seven days, of whom one-third were not armed." You did not take this document into account, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When is this document dated, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 9th of September 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I've never seen this document before. Moreover, I don't see how these documents have any bearing on the number of missing and dead connected with the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me give you my view of the situation and it is very simple. It's easy to take the number of the population that used to reside there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to personalising. His view is not relevant. If he wants to put a view into the question, but constant personalising especially this late in the day is not helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can live with what Mr. Zivanovic has in mind to ask. Proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has made a statement which you don't agree with, can you just put the question to him, trying to confront him with what you think -- what you believe should have been the answer? [Microphone not activated] Relevant matters as they might relate to the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My first question: The number of the population in Srebrenica in July 1995, is that relevant for your findings, for your report, before the fall of the enclave, that is?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a very limited extent because I was asked to estimate the total number of missing and dead persons, not a proportion of those who were in Srebrenica before the fall of the enclave. If I'd been asked that, that -- then it would have been relevant but that was not my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, your task was just to collate the list of the missing persons and compare that list with the census results?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not tasked to compare it with the census. That was something I thought of myself, that it would be a very useful tool. I was asked to check the lists of missing persons and add -- combine different lists and check the quality and come up with the total number as well as a list of all the individuals that had been reported as missing, and that list, with 7.775 persons, I believe, was appended to the 2000 report in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in concluding that two things were not asked from you: Firstly the number that resided in Srebrenica before the fall of the enclave, and the number of people who left Srebrenica after the fall of the enclave? These two things were not asked from you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. According to my records, there are no other Defence teams that wish to cross-examine this witness. If I am wrong, but I am not, then Mr. McCloskey, do you have any re-examination, redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Dr. Brunborg, you're free to go back to the fjords of Norway. We are finished with your testimony. I thank you once more for having returned to continue and finish your testimony after your first visit on the 1st of February. You will receive the attention you need from our staff to facilitate your return back home. On behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can also ask that Professor Radovanovic be excused as well and if the usher can assist in escorting her out we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And I also wish to take this opportunity to thank you, Madam, for having come over and assisted so capably the various Defence teams that have asked you for your help. And I'm sure we will see you again. Thank you. Madam Usher, perhaps you can escort her too. I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Exhibits? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have the list that's been handed to everyone. It's the accurate list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I have two pages here. I don't think I need to go through each and every one of these exhibits unless someone asks me to. This, I take it, has been circulated amongst the Defence teams. Are there any objections to the admission of any of these documents from any of the Defence teams? Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to tender 1D312 and 1D314 in the bundle of 3A. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't just have better eyesight than I do but you also work at a faster speed. We will come to your document, to your exhibit. For the time being I'm just restricting myself to the Prosecution exhibits. Any objection from the Defence teams? We hear none. One question to you, Mr. McCloskey. Having a cursory look at them, I take it that none of them needs translation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They should not, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think they should but I just want a confirmation from you. Mostly they are lists and reports and charts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. This is mostly Mr. Brunborg's work product or international agency work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The registrar will surf through these documents and make sure that none need to have translation, none need to be translated otherwise they will be marked for identification. Failing that they will all be admitted accordingly as Prosecution exhibits by our staff. Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, unless you've changed your mind, I take it that you have one document you wish to tender? Two?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One in its entirety, 1D312, and the other part only partly, paragraph 3(a) of 1D314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Don't you think we also ought to have the heading so that we have the date and what the title of the document is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be the first part of the first page, if it has a heading because I don't know if it has a heading. We just saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it would be more convenient to have the entire document admitted because it's not long. I don't want to create any problems when it comes to the understanding of the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does anyone object to that? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No I agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So these two documents are being admitted. The first one I think still requires translation. Is that correct, Mr. Zivanovic? You yourself have said that you handed it over for translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I will check what's happened. I asked for the translation yesterday and I'm sure it's forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just wanted to check the origin or where these documents came from. Were these Prosecution collection? I didn't -- wasn't able to see ERN numbers or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the source of that document, please, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D312 is not from the Prosecutor's collection. This was obtained from our investigator from Banja Luka through the Commission of Republika Srpska for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, and the other has been taken from the IDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, it means that the Commission of Republika Srpska for Cooperation has not handed you all the documents it should. Am I correct in that interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, they may have and we may have it and we'll check our sources. If there is something else we will get back to Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have it, it needs to be disclosed in a proper manner, please. I take it that you -- if you inquire further you should find it. So we can close the chapter on Dr. Brunborg's testimony and move to the next witness. I take it Mr. Ostojic, you don't have any documents? You do not wish to tender any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the document we used is already in evidence so we have no other documents to tender at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And Madam Fauveau? Thank you. And Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same for us, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I wonder if I might say something briefly before the witness is brought here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In open or in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In open session. He's testifying without protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It's simply to say that we were advised a short while ago by the witnesses unit that when they were with the witness early this afternoon, he seemed rather overwhelmed and at that stage they weren't sure if he was in a state to testify. Now, I've spoken to him and, with a translator, and he seems to be okay and is happy to come in here to testify but I would say that he, during proofing, had seemed pretty nervous. It's the first time, I think, that he's travelled this far abroad and I just wanted to draw that to your attention and also to lead on from that to say that while talking with him, he indicated that insofar as his memories are not clear and that maybe he will need to refresh his memory that he would be more comfortable to him if his statement or relevant part of his statement were to be read back to him rather than him reading it on the computer screen himself. As far as our proofing has gone, it seems that it's maybe something we would have to ask the Court's permission to do and therefore I thought I would raise this at the outset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Elderkin. Are there any remarks from the Defence teams? Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. As long as the proper procedure is followed and that the witness seems not to remember something and then my colleague makes a proper application, of course we will not object for the witness to be reminded of his statement but not without first going through the motion of at least ensuring that it is something that indeed he does not remember. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and what I suggest we do first, following what Mr. Elderkin has pointed out, is for you, Madam Usher, or Madam Registrar, we'll have a short break, if you could make a contact with the victims and witnesses representative, who is assisting the witness, and report back to us if there is anything they wish to alert us to or if he's in a condition to testify. Either of you. It could be Madam Usher. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could be excused for just one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just thought I should add something to this debate. We have kindly been provided with notes of Mr. Elderkin's proofing session with this witness and I'm perfectly happy to see how we go along but this is the position as I understand it: He has seen his witness statement during the course of a proofing session and he has said that he does not now recollect much of what is in there. So that's the position that we are at. It's been shown to him in a room probably in a hotel and he says, I don't remember that. So the Prosecution aren't going to be taken by surprise if he says it again now. He's already told them he doesn't know what's in his witness statement. So I think we ought to be aware of the position we are at at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very good point, Mr. Haynes. I think we will need to hear what the witness has to say about that, because anything could have happened since he was proofed by -- he may have looked at the statement again and refreshed, jogged his memory or he may still suffer from loss of memory or lack of memory. Yes, Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I may say two things. One is that we were initially unsure how well the witness could read. He says that he can read reasonably well, but insofar as he's gone over his statement it's been done orally rather than -- with him reading it. The second point is insofar as we provided a proofing note to the Defence it's incorrect to say that he's substantially forgotten a lot of the statement he made. There are some changes he had identified. Apart from that I would rather elicit from him what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin. Let's not assume anything because we still have to see the witness walk in the courtroom, make the solemn declaration and then it's your task to start putting questions to him. If he shows loss of memory on the events, well, I think we are all experienced here to know how to proceed, and to what limit one could go. Beyond that, I don't think there is a solution. Yes. One question before we proceed. Did you consider whether it's the case of reminding the witness of his rights under Rule 90 or 90(E) or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It was not something that I had done, Mr. President, but if Your Honours would like to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm asking. I have no reason on the basis of the scanty information that we receive --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: To be cautious, I would say yes, if we could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm the Presiding Judge and on behalf of my colleagues, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost and Judge Stole, I wish to welcome you to this courtroom where you are going to give evidence. Let's hope that your evidence doesn't last long. We'll do our utmost to make it come to an end as soon as we can. In the meantime, I need to tell you something which is very important. Our rules require that before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration, you enter to a commitment with us, in a solemn manner, that you will be testifying the truth as we proceed. The text is being handed to you by Madam Usher. Please read it out. Let's hear you read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Is this the first time you are testifying in this Tribunal, Mr. Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the first time. Either here or in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You must be pretty excited. And nervous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good to hear. That's good to hear. We will try to make your life as simple as possible here. Still everyone is doing his duty and there will be several lawyers that will be putting questions to you. The first to go will be Mr. Elderkin and I know that you have met him already. He shouldn't take much -- too much time to finish his examination-in-chief. He will then be followed by some of the Defence lawyers, who also are not expected to take a long time. So if things go well, you should be out and returning home pretty soon. As we go along, you will be asked questions, as I explained. Now, from what we have read, you seem to have lived a part of the events that this Trial Chamber and this trial is interested, is concerned, with. And since I only know part of the information, the rest you will be telling us, I have an obligation to explain one very important right that you enjoy under our rules, namely that, although I have told you that you will be asked questions by various lawyers and you need to answer those questions, there may be times when questions are put to you which, if you answer, may prove detrimental to you, may expose you in your mind, at least, to possible criminal proceedings. I don't know if this is the case. Let's hope that this is not the case. But if it is the case, if there is any question that is put to you that you would prefer not to answer because in your mind it could expose you to problems later on, then you are free to ask the Trial Chamber to exempt you from answering such questions. Now, we will consider, of course, what you would have to say and we will take a decision. The decision may well be to accept your request and exempt you from giving evidence or we may not agree with you and we order you to give your answer. If we do order you to give your answer, however, that answer, whatever you state, will then not be possible to use in any proceedings against you. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Are we ready to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. First of all, please say your name.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Jevto Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How old are you, Mr. Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you identify yourself as a Bosnian Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: In Gornja Pilica, Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you still live there?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's still my residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you've been a farmer all your life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the war in the 1990s in Bosnia, and to start, can you say in what unit you performed your military service in that war?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: In the battalion. I don't know the name of the unit. There was the Lokanj Battalion and the Pilica Battalion. I don't know the name of the units. And I was in the work platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And was your battalion part of any brigade?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said you were in the work platoon. Who was the platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Radivoje Lakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do you know what his rank was?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a captain. This is the rank that he had obtained from the former army when he served in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can I ask, did your workers platoon generally work in one particular location?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: We prepared food for the troops, and when necessary, we went to the front lines to dig the trenches there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the place you prepared food for the troops, did it have a name?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Food? You're talking about food?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the translation is going correctly but I may lead on this small point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Bogdanovic, look at me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not at Mr. Elderkin. At me. Right opposite. Here. You've just explained to Mr. Elderkin that part of the workers -- works platoon was to prepare for the troops and, when necessary, you also went to the front lines to dig the trenches there. Mr. Elderkin wants to know in which place you and your colleagues used to prepare food for the troops. In which place? Where would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We prepared food at Branjevo and then they took the food up there to be distributed, up there at the trenches, Duge Njive, and various other places.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't get the names of the places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are the names of the places important, Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to your next question, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a few questions about how you actually performed your military service day to day. Did your commander have a roll call every day?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean of the work platoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did he do that?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: At the farm in Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And at any particular place at the farm?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: At the farm?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was there a particular building or place at the farm where the commander carried out the daily roll call?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: There was the infirmary there, and there were also three barns there where cows and pigs were kept, and we had the roll call at the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you describe where in relation to Captain Lakic's house this infirmary was?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Where? What do you mean? The location of what? You mean the farm?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I want to ask where the infirmary, where roll call took place, was in relation to Captain Lakic's house.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: 50 metres. That's where the infirmary was. That's where the roll call was done. And his house was quite close to this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened if someone didn't report for work at roll call?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he'd send the police officers to get him. He'd make a phone call. They would come. And then they would put the man in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember if these police officers you mention were civilian or military police?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Which ones? No. It was not the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You mentioned just now there were some barns where cows and pigs were kept. Were those animals raised by people in the workers platoon?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They -- these were the employees who worked there at the farm. They fed these livestock and they had tractors and they grew the crops. And we took only one plot of land where we grew crops for the purpose of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where in relation again to Captain Lakic's house was the area where you grew crops for the military?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very close, in the immediate vicinity, of Lakic's house, just across the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, I hate to interrupt, but I'm -- it's just a suggestion that I'm making. Perhaps we could again simplify the whole process for the witness. We have seen maps and also other documents that give an indication of where the various buildings that you are referring him to were situated. That includes also the approach roads. Perhaps if we -- that is readily available, we could resort to that and he can point them out and it will be easier for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: With your indulgence, Mr. President, in fact I can move just to two or three simple questions that do with buildings. I don't need to identify on a map which I think may cause problems but simply then to follow up with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. It was just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You mentioned animals being raised by employees of the farm.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Pigs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did members of the workers platoon help raise any pigs?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. We grew cabbage, peppers, tomatoes, potatoes, tobacco, and then we took all that up to the kitchen by tractor and there we prepared food for the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was there a part of the farm -- or a farm of which the Branjevo Military Farm was part that belonged to Agroprom?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did the workers platoon use any Agroprom buildings for storage or for taking their meals or for any other activity?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. None of our stuff went into the barns or was put in storage there. We simply picked the vegetables and we transported it up to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And where did you eat your own meals? Was there a particular place?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: At Branjevo, in front of the infirmary. We would get half a loaf of bread per person and one tin, one to two tins of meat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Concerning your work at the farm, can I just ask you if you normally returned to your home at the end of each working day?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After 3.00. Our working hours were from 7.00 until 3.00. And we spent as much time at Branjevo as the troops in the trenches, in two shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about a new topic. And please, if you can now focus on July of 1995. First of all, do you remember learning that Srebrenica had been taken over by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do you remember whether that event occurred on or around a particular holiday?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the 12th of July, St. Peter's Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving an order a few days after St. Peter's Day to go to a school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And where were you when you first heard about the order to go to a school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: I was at home, and then I was told that I should go to the school because some people had been brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who was it who told you this order?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Radivoje Lakic sent some people from the workers platoon, two men came and said, "Well, Radivoje Lakic sent us. Some people had been brought to the school."

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember who those two men were?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Stevo Ostojic and Rajo Jurosevic. They were together with me in the workers platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Which school were you ordered to go to?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: To Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do you know if that school has any other name?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Tesla. That's the Nikola Tesla school. And it's popularly known as Kula or the tower, because there is a tower standing there. It was built hundreds of years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Once you had been given the order, did you go to the Kula school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: We? No, we did not. We just stood there at the door to prevent them from escaping.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: From the time you received the order at your home from your two colleagues, did you then go from home to the school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the school, did you see other members of your workers platoon there?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did any members of the works platoon go with you to the school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? Well, perhaps the reason for the fact that they were not there was because it was closer for them to get there from Lokanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was your commander, Captain Lakic, at the school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you see any other soldiers at the school, whether you recognised them individually or not?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't recognise any of them. I didn't even know what brigade or company they were from. But there were soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the school, what were you told to do?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to put them on buses so that they can be taken -- driven away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you given orders when you arrived to stand guard?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We stood guard there at the school, so that these people could be put on the buses, and then driven some place else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember who told you to stand guard when you got to the school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how should I know? There were some soldiers there. They lined us up there, and they told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did your commander himself tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No. You mean Radivoje?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you go to stand guard? Can you describe in relation to the school building, if possible?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: At the entrance, at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Is this door on the side of the road or the side away from the road?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the -- towards the road. There is a large iron gate, and that's where they were put, and we guarded them there. And then outside of the window, there was the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: From the position where you were standing guard, could you see into the school at all?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you see people inside the school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the windows are pretty low. So we could see them quite easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How many people could you see inside?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how should I know? I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Would you say there were few people or many people, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was quite crowded and they were -- when they were loaded on the buses, the buses were crammed too, so I can't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What kind of clothing were these people wearing? Were they military clothing or were they wearing civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian clothing. They were in -- some were in their underwear, vests. Some wore their boots. Whatever they happened to have on. But they were civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how were these people arranged inside the school? Were they standing or seated?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: They were seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember what the temperature was like that day, the weather?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe 20 degrees. It was a warm day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were the conditions like for the people inside the school? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were thirsty. They were hungry. We gave them some water through the window for them to drink and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know how these people had been brought to the school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: By bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you see any buses then?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw four buses on my way from my house, and that's where they were put on and taken from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this needs some clarification. The buses, the four buses that you saw on your way from your house, which direction were they going to? Were they going to the direction of the school at -- Kula school, or were they coming from that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know where they had come from but they were leaving from the school towards the hall. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That the answer is still not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I intervened, Mr. Elderkin, because your question was directed as to whether he knew where they had been brought from or how they had been brought over to the school. He's your witness. I give him back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your assistance, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic, you just said that -- now, talking about the buses leaving the school -- that they were leaving from the school towards the hall. Which hall do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the hall in Pilica. So they were taken from the school to Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Again talking about this afternoon that you spent on guard at the school in Kula, do you recall seeing any bodies that day in or around the school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, around the school, nine bodies, dead bodies. That's what I stated in 2005, when I gave my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were these bodies, if you can describe again, in relation to the school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: 50 metres from the school, to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what happened to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: To the left of the road, 50 metres from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What happened to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were put on a tractor-trailer and taken away. When the live ones were taken away, then the dead bodies were put on the tractor-trailer and also taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who was lifting those bodies into the tractor-trailer?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: We did. They forced us to do that, to put the bodies in there, and then they made a man to drive the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: While you were on guard that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: We, we, the locals. We loaded them. And then this man drove the tractor away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were on guard, did the prisoners leave the school?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were leaving, slowly, and we stood there, stood guard, lest they should escape, and they simply put them away, put them there, two by two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Elderkin, hasn't been covered. There were three of them from the workers group that went to Kula school, the witness, Stevo and Rajo. Mr. Bogdanovic, were you armed? Were you given a weapon? Were you given a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you were sent to guard these prisoners without carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Finally, the day that you were on guard, what time did you go home that day?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: At around 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next set of questions I have concern the following day and a discrete set of events. It would be worthwhile having them all in one block. I'm not sure if the five minutes is a bit too short. It won't be much more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you wish, Mr. Elderkin. Mr. Bogdanovic, we are going to have a short break, which will give you time to rest a bit. And then we will continue. Madam Usher, if you could kindly escort the witness. One matter, I wanted to alert you to before we break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: About half an hour ago we finished the exhibit process, tendering process, in relation to Dr. Brunborg, and we admitted all the documents that were tendered. It's being suggested to us that P02416, P02417, P02418 and P02422 should be admitted -- should be kept under seal. Is there any opposition to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So those four documents, I don't need to repeat the 65 ter number, will be kept under seal. Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Elderkin. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic, I'd like to talk to you now about the following day, the day after you were on guard at the Kula school. That next morning, did you go to work at the Branjevo Military Farm?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did Captain Lakic have a roll call that morning?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a roll call and said that we should go there because some people had been brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where was it that he said you should go?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: He said that at the infirmary, which was our assembly point. This is where we all got together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And when he spoke to you at the infirmary that morning, where was it that he told you you had to go to that day? What place?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: That we should go to Pilica because some people had been brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you go to Pilica?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he actually went there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And as well as you and Captain Lakic, did the other members of the work platoon go with you?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember any of their names, the ones who came with you?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe two or three of them, because there were some other people from other villages and I don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names that you do remember?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Jovan Ilic, Rajo Jurosevic and Stevo Ostojic. These are the three names that I know. And Vojo Lakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: As you walked from the Branjevo Military Farm to the Pilica Dom that morning, do you remember seeing anything unusual along the side of the road or near the road?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: We saw some dead bodies, people who had been shot to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you see those bodies?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: As you go from the farm towards Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you say how many bodies you saw?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: About 10 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what kind of clothes were they wearing? Again, were they civilian clothes, military clothes?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Pilica Dom -- sorry, if I could rephrase. Being from Pilica, is the dom a building that you know well?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was this building normally used for?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a youth hall and some shows would be presented there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What kind of rooms were there inside the dom?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: It was quite simple. There was just one hall, kind of a sports hall or a gym, just one room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That morning, when you arrived at the dom, were there any soldiers there other than your works platoon colleagues?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you tell what kind of soldiers they were, for example, infantry or military police or civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: They were soldiers. I don't really know what unit they belonged to, what battalion. How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were those soldiers doing when you arrived at the dom?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were securing the area. They didn't allow the locals, the villagers, to get in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And for the securing operation, could you see who appeared to be conducting it or who was in charge, the civilian authorities or the army?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. We just loaded and took things out of the hall. I don't know who was in command of the overall operation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Other than your works platoon colleagues, did you recognise anybody else there?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was your commander, Captain Lakic, there?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was there for as long as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the dom, did Captain Lakic give you any orders? Is that okay? Can you hear okay now?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'll ask my question again. When you arrived at the dom, did Captain Lakic give you any orders?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He ordered us to load the dead bodies on to the two trucks that had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how you carried out this loading? Where the trucks were, what it was you did to get the bodies into these trucks?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: The trucks reversed to the -- into the gate and then we put some planks on and we -- we put the bodies on. We reversed the truck to the gate, put two thick planks and then the two of us would grab each body, one would grab the arms and the other one would grab the legs and then we would just load them on to the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about the trucks. Can you describe them, their size, the kind of vehicle they were?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: They were yellow. They were tipper trucks. I don't know if you know that. They are used to carry gravel, that kind of cargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know who was driving the trucks that day?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who drove the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who else was carrying the corpses with you?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Apart from you, who was also carrying the bodies into the trucks?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the workers platoon. There were 12 of them and I don't know why it is that not one of them wants to admit to that fact. It will turn out in the end that I was the only one who was doing that, that I was the only man there doing that. And yet there were 12 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, I know this subject matter I'm talking about this day is difficult, but please say at any point if you do want to have a break. I'll continue to ask questions but please let me know if you want to have a few minutes. You talked about loading corpses into the trucks.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you want to make a break, you can go ahead. But...

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Would you like to, sir?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Would you like to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic, look at me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, don't ask me. If you want, you just do whatever you want. Don't make a break on my account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. And Mr. Bogdanovic, if you at any time feel tired or you wish us to stop, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were the corpses --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were the corpses you were loading? Were they inside the dom or outside?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: They were inside the dom. They were piled up on each other, just lying there scattered all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was anyone alive in there?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were their bodies of men only or were there bodies of men and women?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Only two women, only two women.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The bodies that you saw, were they dressed in military clothing or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies, civilian, civilian clothing. They were all dressed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: From what you saw inside the dom that day, did it appear to you that those people were killed in the dom or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: In the dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: This next question, it may not be easy for you but I would ask if you could please describe the condition of the bodies that you and your Pilica-Lokanj Battalion colleagues from moving out of the dom. Please, could you tell the Judges, even if it is difficult for you, what the condition was of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just wonder this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I don't know what he is after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think for the time being we need to proceed and then if it obviously turns out not to be relevant we'll stop. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, I think he's already answered the question when he said that the bodies were dead. And to go any further than that, the Prosecution is just trying to raise sympathy and inflame --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let us direct the orchestra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Mr. Bogdanovic, I think I will read out again the question that Mr. Elderkin put to you. It's a very simple one, if you can answer it. "What was the condition of these bodies that you saw there at the Pilica Dom?" You have already told us that they were dead, all dead. What else can you tell us about how --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, some were curled up, some were stretched out. There was this huge pile and they were piled up, one over another. They were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How was it that you and your colleagues carrying the bodies were able to keep going with that kind of work that day?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: It was close. The trucks reversed all the way to the door. We then mounted two wooden boards from the door to the truck, and then we dragged the body up the wooden boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you drinking anything that day to sustain yourself?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where was your commander, Captain Lakic, during this time?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: He was there, close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time of the day it was that you finished this work?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you were drinking that day, could you say what it was you were drinking?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Rakija brandy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you get that?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Neighbours, the locals, brought that to us. We drank for courage, to be able to sustain looking at the blood and the bodies, and the brains of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: During the course of that day, did you hear anybody mention a number of how many bodies were in the dom?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard somebody on the road saying that there were 550, but we ourselves did not count.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: But based on your work that day, does that number seem a reasonable number to you?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it does. It should.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Excuse me for one moment, Mr. President, if I could ask my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic, thank you for talking about that day for us. I just want to ask a few more questions, back in the more general period, to do with your work at the Branjevo Farm, and I want to start by asking if you remember talking to myself, my colleagues, in the last two days and talking about the work and the places you worked at the farm?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? After those days? When?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you recall talking with me and some of my colleagues yesterday and today about your work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd just like to know where this is going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Where is it going, Mr. Elderkin? So far we haven't had any indications of -- why don't you go straight to the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I can explain where it's going certainly, Mr. President. The location of the killings that took place at the farm took place in certain areas. We want to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I could in that case ask for a photograph which is in page 212 of Exhibit P02103 to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic, please could I ask you to look --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- at the photograph that should be appearing on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You mean this photo? This is Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Branjevo, the farm, Ekonomija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In the photograph, did you see there are two long, low buildings at the left-hand side of the photograph. Can you say what --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the barns, the cow-sheds and this is the Bijeljina-Zvornik road. And this is where the road forks off towards the farm buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And are these buildings on the land of the military farm?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were these two barns or stables used for, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: For cattle and for pigs and for horses. That's where they were fed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember if members or any other member of your workers platoon went to these buildings ever?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What did they do in these buildings?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: In this building here, we stored corn, maize and this is the garage, their garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you talking about the single building to the right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: This is where we cleaned the corn and this is where the pigs were and this is where the cattle was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need the usher's assistance. Let's start more or less from the beginning. Can he, with the gadget that they had given you, point, mark, the two buildings that you said were the places, the cow, the barns, the cow-sheds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you put an X on both of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will I be able to do that? [Marks] Ah, I am. And you want me to put something here as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If you could use perhaps a circle for the other building. I'm not sure I'm seeing anything on -- could you tell us first, Mr. Bogdanovic, the two buildings marked with X, you told us that workers would go to those buildings to raise cattle, those are the two with the X you've identified?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And there is a third building in the picture, just to their right. Could you tell us what that building was used for by members of the workers platoon?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: This one here? This one here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If could you draw a circle there, I think it is that one.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What did the works platoon use that building for?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't use it for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who did use that building?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Only -- the workers who used to serve things on the farm used it. This is the Semberija agriculture combine who gave us three or four hectares of land to use to grow crops on that land for the military, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can you see on this photograph, or can you say in relation to this photograph, otherwise the place where you used to eat your lunches?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: When it was raining, we used to eat here where this door is. This is where we took shelter from the rain. The cattle was here and if it was raining we would go find shelter over there. And this is where the tractors and other agricultural machinery was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Would you please mark with an arrow the door you mentioned just now where you said you'd eat in the rain?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And finally, I don't need to ask you any more to use the magic pen but could you tell us how far it is from these two barns to the infirmary or to Captain Lakic's house?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: About 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Excuse me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdanovic, thank you very much. You should be asked to sign your name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just his initials would suffice. Just your initials, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What kind of letters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, J for Jevto and B for Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Top left or right, wherever you like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we require today's date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If Mr. Bogdanovic wouldn't mind writing it. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could put 10, 5, 07, that's today's date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Bogdanovic. And thank you, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We've got 15 minutes to go. I have on my list the Popovic, Beara, Nikolic and Pandurevic teams that have asked for 20 minutes each. Let's start with you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have also noticed Ms. Fauveau on -- you asked for ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any questions for this witness, but I would like to ask for five minutes before we adjourn to raise an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Beara team?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Nikolic team? Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have some questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. And if you could stop, limit yourself to about eight minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doesn't mean to say if you're not finished you will not continue tomorrow. Don't misunderstand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You've been asked questions by the Prosecution as to how difficult it was for you to remove these bodies from the dom on that day. But the Prosecution failed to ask you the most important question. I suggest to you that either yourself and the people that were with you, you had absolutely nothing to do with those bodies that were in the dom at that day; is that correct, Mr. Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? What connection are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm simply suggesting to you that you don't know who killed those people and you had nothing to do with those killings. You were just asked to go and carry bodies, nothing else?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No connection whatsoever. Of course, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's what I thought was important for you to mention, that you had nothing to do with that, because the Prosecution failed to ask you that question. Now --

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my next question is you mentioned something about seeing some bodies at the school the day prior to that?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you said that you were forced to carry those bodies on to some kind of a truck or a trailer.

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a tractor-trailer and they were driven away, nine pieces, nine human bodies. I don't know what to call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And those people, Mr. Bogdanovic, who forced you to do that, those are the soldiers that you didn't know who they were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who they were, what brigade, who they were. I don't know who brought them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the bodies that you saw going to -- going to the dom on the second day, you mentioned seeing ten bodies in the field. I take it that you also had nothing to do with the death of these people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: We saw that in the morning on the way to the dom, and on the following day, when we came to load them, they were gone when we came from Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you have nothing to do with the death of these people, do you?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You don't know when or how they were killed?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: They were not killed by anybody from Zvornik, the battalion or -- I don't know. I really -- I don't know where they came from. I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you yourself, Mr. Bogdanovic, you never went into that school, did you?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in response to a question by my colleague that you could see some people inside the school, just like you knew -- can you confirm whether this was on the ground floor or the first floor that you could see people through the window?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: The first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if you can just look at me for one moment, on the first floor meaning -- Mr. Bogdanovic, here. So when you say first floor, I mean you were looking up through the window, is that what you mean by looking at the first floor?

utterances.speaker: JEVTO BOGDANOVIC
utterances.text: The first floor is the ground floor actually. And they were all on the first floor, in the gym. They were not on the upper floor. And that's why we could see them. The windows are quite large so we could look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bogdanovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Mr. Haynes, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
